Gaussian naive Bayes estimates a mean and variance per class/feature; multinomial naive Bayes estimates smoothed token probabilities from nonnegative feature counts. Both add log priors to summed feature log likelihoods, avoiding probability underflow. A variance floor handles constant Gaussian features; Laplace smoothing prevents unseen tokens from zeroing an entire class likelihood. Conditional independence is an approximation, so probabilities may be poorly calibrated.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** The posterior score is $\log P(c)+\sum_j\log P(x_j|c)$ under conditional independence. For multinomial counts with Laplace smoothing, $P(j|c)=(N_{cj}+\alpha)/(\sum_lN_{cl}+\alpha V)$. Smoothing avoids zero probabilities, while log space avoids multiplying many tiny values. Independence misspecification can still make the resulting probabilities overconfident. [3](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://jakevdp.github.io/PythonDataScienceHandbook/05.05-naive-bayes.html) and [2](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive_bayes.html).
